thread.title: FEMA Funding at Risk for Vermont's Rural Communities After Trump Denies Disaster Declaration Request
thread.title_full: FEMA Funding at Risk for Vermont's Rural Communities After Trump Denies Disaster Declaration Request

author: Julia Tilton
title: FEMA Funding at Risk for Vermont's Rural Communities After Trump Denies Disaster Declaration Request
text:
The site of Brattleboro Housing Partnerships’ former development in West Brattleboro, Vermont, is unassuming at first glance. The windows are boarded up, and native tall grass stretches across the property and along the banks of the Whetstone Brook, a tributary to the Connecticut River.
On a Sunday afternoon in early September 2025, Windham Regional Planning Commissioner Chris Campany stood on the bridge that connects the property to Route 9 heading into Brattleboro. Beneath him, water gurgled between a series of granite boulders and then through a large overflow culvert designed to keep water moving during heavy rains.
The culvert and the five-acre restored floodplain that surrounds it were the focus of Campany’s weekend site visit. The infrastructure, which was completed in 2022, is part of a $23.1 million disaster resilience project that was years in the making following severe damage from Tropical Storm Irene in 2011.
Now, the kind of funding that made the Brattleboro floodplain restoration possible could be in jeopardy. On October 24, 2025, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) denied an August 22, 2025 request from Vermont Governor Phil Scott for disaster funding for severe storms and flooding that swept through the state on July 10, 2025. This comes amidst delays in federal disaster response time and the suspension of the FEMA’s Hazard Grant Mitigation Program under President Donald Trump’s administration. Those changes, and the lack of federal aid in Vermont, are leaving the state’s rural communities uncertain about the future of disaster preparedness amidst a pattern of more intense storms.
“We don’t know at all what to expect now,” said Campany. In June, Trump said he wants to “phase out” FEMA after the 2025 hurricane season, transferring the bulk of emergency response services back to the states. Also in June, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who oversees FEMA, began requiring that all FEMA grants and contracts over $100,000 cross her desk for approval. Replacing a culvert costs more than $100,000, Campany said.
With a population of 648,000 people, Vermont has historically relied on federal dollars for disaster response funding that state and local taxes alone can’t produce.
Between 2011-2024, rural counties in Vermont had among the greatest occurrences of federally-declared extreme weather disasters in the country, per a Daily Yonder analysis of data from Atlas of Accountability, a disaster-mapping project of New York University’s Rebuild by Design initiative.
Now, uncertainty at the federal level has prompted Campany and others around the state to consider new approaches to building disaster preparedness and resilience.
Mapping Rural Disasters
In 2011, Tropical Storm Irene damaged 60 of the 80 apartments on Brattleboro Housing Partnership’s property. Following the flooding, 11 buildings were removed from the development, and residents were moved to a new location three miles away out of the floodplain. With the help of federal, state, and local funding, the land where the apartments had once been was then replanted to become a floodplain forest, complete with tall grass.
Just after the floodplain restoration was completed on the Brattleboro Housing Partnership site, Vermont was again hit with catastrophic flooding. Back-to-back summer storm events in 2023, 2024, and 2025 brought unprecedented levels of rainfall to the state. During the 2023 storm, the West Brattleboro floodplain behaved as it was supposed to, slowing the waters of the swollen Whetstone Brook by diffusing the surge across the restored land. By giving the water a place to spread out upstream, the floodplain site helped prevent property damage downstream, where Brattleboro meets the Connecticut River.
“The whole point of this is to give the brook the space it needs to move,” said Campany. “You don’t fight it.”
Across town, another recently restored floodplain site called Kikitta Ahki, a name derived from the Indigenous Abenaki language, serves a similar purpose. Before its restoration in 2024, the 12-acre site bordering the Whetstone Brook had been disconnected from the natural floodplain and filled with gravel. That gravel acted as a barrier for high waters when Tropical Storm Irene hit in 2011, meaning more water was shuttled downstream, where it damaged public infrastructure and more than 50 commercial and residential properties in a town of about 12,000 people.
Like the West Brattleboro site, the Kikitta Ahki restoration was made possible in part with disaster aid and resilience funding from FEMA and the state.
Across the country, extreme-weather-related disaster declarations are made by the President for severe events beyond local or state control, like hurricanes or tornadoes. Once a disaster has received a federal declaration, a state or local government becomes eligible to receive federal disaster relief and mitigation funding.
“In many ways, it’s a political process, but it’s also an economic process,” said Amy Chester, executive director of Rebuild, which was started in 2012 as an initiative of President Barack Obama’s Hurricane Sandy Task Force. Flooding is an expensive type of disaster, Chester said.
A Daily Yonder analysis of Atlas of Accountability data found that in Vermont, natural disasters have prompted significant FEMA spending, with the state’s rural counties receiving a combined $360 million in FEMA public assistance and hazard mitigation funding between 2011-2024. Though disasters occur across rural and urban boundaries, rural counties in Vermont occupy four spots on Rebuild by Design’s list of the top 10 counties with the highest disaster occurrences across the U.S. from 2011-2024.
In order to qualify for FEMA public assistance funding, a county has to cross a $1 million threshold of damage to public infrastructure. Hazard mitigation funding is a separate pool of funding that communities can put toward strengthening infrastructure against future damage in the aftermath of a disaster.
In Vermont, that can look like restoring floodplains or elevating buildings out of harm’s way. Both restoration sites in Brattleboro were made possible in part with hazard mitigation grants from FEMA. Since Trump took office in January, the approvals process for states requesting hazard mitigation funding has been slowed, per a September 19, 2025, analysis from the Carnegie Endowment for Peace. FEMA did not approve any requests for hazard mitigation funding between March and October 24, 2025. During that time, 47 applications for hazard mitigation funding were submitted to the agency, including from Vermont, which had its request denied on October 24.
Though Vermont didn’t see the same level of extreme weather in the summer of 2025 as it did in 2023 and 2024, storms on July 10, 2025, caused flooding and public infrastructure damage in Caledonia and Essex counties. Damages in Caledonia County were more than ten times the qualifying threshold for public assistance, per a September 10 letter that Vermont’s Congressional Delegation sent to the White House reiterating its now-denied August 22 request for FEMA aid.
“No federal assistance is going to come into a state unless the declaration request has been approved,” said Jennifer DeCesaro, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for Peace and coauthor of the September 19 analysis. DeCesaro said that the administration has tended to process the disaster declaration requests in batches over the last several months. On October 24, disaster declaration requests for severe storms and flooding in Maryland, dated August 19, 2025, and Illinois, dated September 15, 2025, were denied in addition to Vermont’s request.
“It’s unclear what the motivation is behind not reviewing and making decisions on disaster declaration requests as they are submitted,” DeCesaro said.
Building for Future Floods
In the valley below Okemo, one of Vermont’s most popular ski resorts, the town of Ludlow sits along the Black River, another tributary to the Connecticut River. On an August afternoon this past summer, Jason Rasmussen walked into Ludlow’s City Hall. Rasmussen is the executive director of the Mount Ascutney Regional Commission, which, like Campany’s organization, provides technical assistance in the aftermath of disasters in southern Windsor County.
Inside the City Hall, FEMA flyers hung from a bulletin board with information about applying for public assistance. During the July storm event in 2023, the Black River swelled beyond its banks, flooding nearby businesses with up to six feet of water in some cases. While many businesses have since been repaired and reopened, Rasmussen said the town is still searching for $26 million to carry out a larger infrastructure project relocating a wastewater treatment plant that’s currently in the floodplain.
“It’s hard for a town of 2,000 people to raise that kind of money,” said Rasmussen. “They need the grants.”
Rasmussen entered the City Hall meeting room where flood insurance rate maps hung on a back wall. These maps, which FEMA puts together, are what make communities eligible for the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). When disasters happen, those who are in the defined floodplain that have experienced damage as a result of flooding can file a claim with the NFIP.
“You get some money, but it’s usually never near enough to pay for the fix,” Rasmussen said.
Part of the problem is that the flood maps don’t provide the full picture of the floodplain, according to Ben Walsh, the climate and energy program director at the Vermont Public Interest Research Group.
“FEMA does not think at all about those little tiny streams and their mapping,” said Walsh. “If you look at Vermont and ignore that, it looks like we’re gonna be just fine. If you look at Vermont and you actually incorporate that, it’s very clear that there are real risks.”
The maps for southern Windsor County haven’t been updated in decades, though FEMA is now working to modernize them. Though Campany said that because the maps are fed with historical data, they’re often missing key pieces of information about what future storms will look like in a changing climate.
“Once they’re updated, they’re already out of date,” Campany said.
Since the 1960s, annual precipitation in Vermont has increased by an average of six inches, with the largest increases occurring in the state’s mountainous regions, according to the state’s climate change website. Over the next several decades, Vermont is projected to see increased winter and spring precipitation with a larger proportion of that precipitation falling as rain due to warming temperatures.
In towns like Ludlow and Brattleboro, these heavy storms can bring millions of dollars of damage in a matter of hours. Campany worries about a future where these communities, and their sparsely-populated neighbors, may have to do with less federal aid. Some towns with populations under 1,000 operate with annual budgets under one million dollars.
“If you have a thunderstorm cell sit on top of you and blow out some culvert or damage a bridge, you may have your entire town budget’s equivalent in damage, resulting from just one isolated cell,” Campany said.
Vermont Looks to the Future
Campany stood along the banks of the brook at Kikitta Ahki as the water caught the first September leaves fluttering down from the canopy. Watching, Campany said he sees his role with the Windham Regional Planning Commission as helping people understand “the new relationship of water on the landscape.”
After the July 2023 floods, the state of Vermont passed the Flood Safety Act, which will move the management of Vermont’s river corridors — including streams and brooks — to the state by 2028. The idea behind river corridor regulation is to better enable the natural need for rivers to move and channels to migrate by limiting where developments can go. Fluvial erosion, or bank erosion, is a particularly violent type of flooding that can wash away the ground and whatever developments sit on top of it. The state is aiming to increase capacity by moving the regulation of these river corridors from a patchwork of towns that have adopted bylaws over 240 individual municipalities to one office at the state level.
“This structure of local governance was established when the Puritans and Pilgrims first landed,” Campany said. “Does it make sense in 2025? Maybe it does for some things, but when it comes to climate adaptation, resilience, and our continued existence of some communities on the landscape, I don’t know how you do it at that scale.”
Beyond management, Vermont has also made moves to diversify its sources of resilience funding in recent years. In May 2024, Vermont passed the Climate Superfund Act, a relatively new model of legislation that allows the state to recover financial damages from fossil fuel companies for the effects of climate change on Vermont. New York has enacted similar legislation.
The idea is that the funds raised would then be used to support adaptation projects, like floodplain restorations, said Walsh, who worked with the Vermont Legislature to pass the Climate Superfund Act.
“Vermonters are not the ones that cause the climate crisis — it’s these oil companies and other fossil fuel companies, and so they should be made to pay their fair share,” Walsh said.
This past May, the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a complaint against Vermont and New York, claiming that their climate superfund acts defy federal law. The DOJ’s actions come after Trump signed an April 8, 2025, Executive Order aimed at “Protecting American Energy From State Overreach.” On September 16, the DOJ filed a motion for a summary judgment, though a decision is still pending.
Despite what happens in court, Walsh and Campany agree there’s a need for more resources to deal with repeat storm events. Federal funding for projects like the Brattleboro Housing Partnership and Kikitta Ahki floodplain restorations completed after Tropical Storm Irene now has a very different outlook under the Trump administration. And while Vermont can try to fill the gaps, costs are often more than the state or its many municipalities can handle with a limited taxpayer base.
Still, at the hyper-local scale, Rasmussen said community members are more aware of flood risks than they were a decade ago.
This opens the door to chipping away at large-scale infrastructure projects, like the $26 million project to relocate Ludlow’s wastewater treatment plant, even if it takes years or a decade to raise the money. After the 2023 floods, Rasmussen said there’s less neighborhood and political resistance than there once was to fundraise for this kind of project.
“I think people are coming around to the fact that it’s kind of a new normal, and we have to do something about it,” Rasmussen said.
